title: Why Are There So Few Black Lawyers in Corporate Law Firms? An Institutional Analysis
pub: California Law Review (84 Calif. L. Rev. 493)
author: David B. Wilkins · G. Mitu Gulati

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: The source supplies a compatible institutional framework in which economic interests are constrained by professional ideology, social capital, inequality and bounded rationality. However, these theoretical premises do not directly assess in-house buyer power, professional capture, reciprocal duties or contextual regulation, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s rejection of size as a sufficient explanation for Big Law’s durability and materially develops it through a multi-causal institutional account of growth, leverage, monitoring, training and promotion. It further shows that inherited pyramid and up-or-out arrangements are not demonstrably superior to alternative staffing and management structures.
qs: 19961                WHY ARE THERE SO FEW BLACK LAWYERS         There is, however, no reason to believe that these traditional insti- tutional practices are more efficient than others that might have been developed to respond to the problems elite firms presently face.

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s underlying economics and adds a historical institutional mechanism: shifting routine work to lower-cost paralegals can reduce client costs while increasing firm profits, showing that fewer or cheaper lawyer hours need not reduce margins. It also materially extends the analysis by linking pricing reform to governance, staffing, training and inclusion, while treating those effects as conditional rather than demonstrated.
qs: By increasing the amount of work given to paralegals, firms can simultaneously cut client costs while increasing profits since paralegal hours are directly billed to clients at rates that substantially exceed their costs.

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s systemic account and materially develops it by explaining how selective training, pyramidal production and racialized access to business opportunities make the tournament unequal and extend competition into partnership.
qs: First, contrary to standard tournament theory, firms do not run a competition in which every associate is given an equal chance to succeed.

Given these multi-level partner compensation systems and the ever- present danger that unproductive partners will be fired, many partners effectively do face an almost endless series of promotion contests.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source does not address AI directly, but materially strengthens the cluster’s implementation-focused account by showing that lawyer development and quality assessment require costly senior supervision and discretionary judgment. Its warning that outcomes and time spent are imperfect quality measures supports evaluating complete legal workflows rather than relying on simple productivity proxies.
qs: This apprenticeship model, however, is expensive because it takes senior lawyers away from revenue-generating activities."       Finally, given the importance of discretionary judgment to assess- ing the quality of a lawyer's work, results are not an accurate measure of shirking.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess modern AI capability or verification, but it materially extends the cluster’s work-redesign proposition by showing that technology-driven changes to staffing, pricing and management interact with path-dependent firm structures, training opportunities and racial inequality. It also reinforces that restructuring has no predetermined outcome and may reproduce disadvantage without deliberate operating-model and incentive redesign.
qs: Firms that adopt more rationalized manage- ment structures may simply ghettoize black lawyers in relatively low status positions.

st.t: Cravath model: Modern firms retain hollowed labels
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis that the Cravath model arose from historically contingent conditions, persisted after those conditions changed, and continues to shape firm structures despite departures from its original practices. It also reinforces the synthesis’s rejection of presumed efficiency and meritocracy, while supporting incremental institutional reform rather than inevitability.
qs: The first ignores the fact that our existing institutions are the product of historical traditions and contingencies, and may very well be less suited to contemporary conditions than plausible alternatives.

st.t: Legal judgment: Correct output may remain insufficient
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s underlying claim that technically correct legal work may be insufficient because effective lawyering requires contextual, discretionary judgment beyond specialised knowledge. It also reinforces the cluster’s qualification that judgment is central without being uniquely legal or objectively measurable. It does not address AI-specific verification or whether assisted performance develops supervisory expertise.
qs: Good judgment in this context derives from, but ultimately tran-  scends, specialized knowledge and technical expertise.

kp.k: Institutional incentives can sustain racial exclusion despite competition
kp.d: This 1996 article concerns racial inequality and corporate law firm organization, not AI. The authors propose that high salaries, pyramidal staffing and selective training can insulate discriminatory employment decisions from competitive penalties. Where firms can substitute average white lawyers for equally capable black lawyers without reducing productivity, market competition need not eliminate discrimination. This is a theoretical institutional account, supported provisionally rather than established conclusively by the evidence presented.
qs: Average workers are merely being substituted for average workers.
We therefore do not claim to have proven anything. Instead, we offer our data, as we offer our model, as an invitation to discussion and further work.

kp.k: Historical representation data establish the problem's scale
kp.d: The article reports National Law Journal figures indicating that, as of 1995, more than 1,641 black lawyers worked in the nation's 250 largest firms, including 351 partners. The corresponding 1996 survey placed black representation at 2.4% of lawyers and just over one percent of partners. The authors argue that underrepresentation must be assessed against the relevant qualified applicant pool, while questioning whether firms' conventional credentials accurately define that pool.
qs: blacks constituted just 2.4% of the lawyers in corpo- rate firms, and, more importantly, just over one percent of the partners.
statistics can not answer the question of whether blacks are underrepresented in corporate firms.

kp.k: Professional judgment makes quality assessment costly
kp.d: The authors argue that legal competence depends on discretionary judgment and practical experience, making recruitment predictions, supervision and evaluation expensive. Outcomes and hours worked are imperfect measures of work quality. They consequently explain high wages and promotion tournaments as substitutes for some direct monitoring, not as mechanisms that eliminate the need for it.
qs: good lawyering is a practice that ultimately cannot be reduced to principles or rules that can be taught in the classroom.
Direct monitoring, however, is expensive.
These alternatives fall into two general categories: high wages and tournaments.

kp.k: High wages motivate effort beyond partnership ambitions
kp.d: The article explains premium associate pay as attracting a large applicant pool and discouraging shirking through the risk of losing a scarce, well-paid position. This mechanism also applies to associates who do not intend to compete for partnership. The authors report that starting salaries exceeded $85,000 in New York and comparable cities and cite research finding a roughly $11,000 annual large-firm premium after adjustments for measured differences. These are historical figures, not contemporary compensation claims.
qs: Many students state that the high salaries paid by corporate firms are the primary reason they choose jobs in this sector over what they consider to be more rewarding work in government or public interest practice.
an associate lawyer in the largest firm-size category makes roughly $11,000 more per year than her counterpart in the smallest firm-size category.

kp.k: Pyramidal production separates routine work from professional development
kp.d: The authors describe firms decomposing matters into routine tasks and judgment-intensive work, assigning the former to cheaper junior personnel. Associate leverage generates profits and enables firms to tolerate turnover, but firms still require trained senior associates and replacement partners. Increasing use of paralegals illustrates that many tasks previously reserved for lawyers do not require traditional elite legal credentials.
qs: Partners make money on the surplus of revenues generated by associ- ates over the amount they are paid.
Given their pyramid structure, however, it is grossly inefficient for firms to train all of their associates.
Today, much of this work is done by people who have no legal education whatsoever.

kp.k: Selective training undermines the equal-opportunity tournament model
kp.d: The article distinguishes a training track, providing demanding work and developmental relationships, from a flatlining track dominated by routine assignments. Training is both a firm-wide benefit and a private investment for individual partners, who have incentives to favor associates likely to benefit their own practices. Initial advantages become self-reinforcing; untrained associates become increasingly difficult to bill at rising seniority-based rates. Partnership selection therefore reflects unequal opportunities to develop, not merely discovery of pre-existing ability.
qs: Associate training is both a public good for the firm and a private good for individual partners.
Training is the Royal Jelly of elite law firms.
firms do not run a competition in which every associate is given an equal chance to succeed.

kp.k: Recruiting signals serve prestige as well as staffing
kp.d: The authors argue that firms recruit both to obtain workers and to advertise institutional quality to clients, competitors and recruits. Academic credentials dominate visible screening, while personality and fit dominate less visible selection. Firms collect little substantive evidence about candidates' legal skills despite extensive recruiting expenditure. The authors contend that this combination can exclude capable black candidates, discount their credentials and encourage investment in visible signals rather than useful skills.
qs: Elite law firms have two primary objectives in hiring. The first is to stock the pipeline with associates capable of competently filling the firm's labor needs. The second is to signal the firm's quality to clients, competitors, and potential recruits.
It is the need for foot-soldiers, not generals, that drives the hiring process.

kp.k: Preliminary surveys identify barriers but cannot establish causation
kp.d: The authors examined directory records for 60 black Harvard graduates from 1981–1982 and 57 from 1987–1988, received 66 responses to a survey sent to approximately 200 black alumni, and requested entering-class information from 250 firms. Table 3 reports 73 responding firms and 96 black entering associates, 23 of whom attended Harvard. The authors explicitly acknowledge small samples, potential selection bias, possible overlap and the absence of comparable white Harvard graduate data; the results are not claimed to be statistically significant.
qs: We make no claims that the results of our analysis are statistically significant or that they meet the relevant stan- dards for empirical research.
In addi- tion, we do not have comparable data on white Harvard Law School graduates.

kp.k: Mentoring and work allocation are central retention barriers
kp.d: Among the 66 black Harvard survey respondents, 26 reported partner interest in their careers, 40 reported difficulty getting good assignments, and 26 of those 40 said this worsened over time. Twenty-seven of the 40 without mentoring identified its absence as a factor in departure. The authors link these reports to affinity-based mentoring, stereotypes, token visibility and expectations of early departure, while distinguishing respondents' perceptions from independently established differential treatment.
qs: Black associates face three significant barriers to getting on the training track.
Blacks consistently report that they have difficulty in forming these supportive relationships.
Even if these respondents are mistaken about this, the fact that they believe it to be true may induce some black associates to embark on the counterpro- ductive career strategies we describe below.

kp.k: Rational defensive strategies can worsen career prospects
kp.d: The authors hypothesize that heightened risks of adverse evaluation and declining lateral opportunities encourage either cautious avoidance of demanding work or risky attempts to demonstrate exceptional ability. Both can reduce access to training and promotion. They describe a possible litigation trap: litigation can offer transferable skills and visible opportunities, yet large teams, routine work, limited client exposure and weak supervision may impede development. Survey respondents were 45% litigators, but the authors acknowledge multiple explanations for that concentration.
qs: Both strategies, however, can end up diminishing a black associate's long term chances for success at the firm.
The lower levels of scrutiny in litigation increase the risk that an associate will fall through the cracks.
litigation is generally less stable than corporate work.

kp.k: Partnership does not end unequal opportunity
kp.d: The article argues that growing pressure to originate business exposes black partners to disadvantages in both external client markets and internal referral networks. Access to influential contacts, reciprocal referrals, mentors and political allies affects survival after promotion. Government or other outside experience can provide an alternative route to partnership, but lateral entry also carries integration risks. The authors warn that partner departures further weaken associate recruitment and mentoring.
qs: Today, to keep their positions, partners must compete for both business and political allies.
Internal referrals are premised on notions of reciprocity, trust, and politics.
The net result, therefore, is that firms are hemorrhaging black lawyers from both ends.

kp.k: Formal remedies must change access and partner incentives
kp.d: The authors assess anti-discrimination litigation, formal training and assignment systems, diversity training, client-demand initiatives and affirmative action. Each can help, but formal programs may leave informal allocation of valuable work unchanged. They recommend extending affirmative efforts beyond recruitment to assignments and development, potentially linking partner compensation and advancement to diversity outcomes. Their discussion of Title VII and affirmative-action legality reflects the legal context of 1996.
qs: Formal training programs cannot sub- stitute for this kind of real experience.
Powerful partners routinely bypass the system to grab superstar associates
If firms are truly serious about improving the pros- pects of their black lawyers, they must implement policies that change the incentives of partners.

kp.k: Client demand can make inclusion economically consequential
kp.d: The authors describe the ABA Minority Counsel Demonstration Program as an attempt to change firms' incentives through client purchasing. They report participation by 133 corporations, 39 major firms and 21 minority-owned firms in its first three years, with minority attorneys collecting more than $100 million in fees. These results concern minorities collectively, not black lawyers alone. The authors caution that nominal client support may produce little substantial work and that corporate purchasing incentives do not automatically align with workforce diversity.
qs: By stimulating demand for the services of minority law- yers at large law firns, the Program seeks, inter alia, "to increase the number of minorities they recruit, hire, retain and promote to partner- ship
Just because a corporation sells its products to a diverse population of customers, however, does not necessarily mean that it will want its lawyers to be diverse as well.

kp.k: Technology and pricing could change viable staffing structures
kp.d: In forward-looking discussion, the authors report proposals for virtual firms, diamond-shaped staffing with more experienced middle-level lawyers, and hourglass structures in which technology reduces middle-level information-processing roles. These are alternative possibilities attributed to commentators, not observed AI effects. They also argue conditionally that fixed fees would make flatlining costly rather than profitable, while teamwork and professional management could improve developmental access.
qs: In a world of fixed fees, flatlining would become a cost to the firm as opposed to a potential source of profit.
Others assert that twenty-first century firms are more likely to resemble "diamonds" rather than pyramids, with a large number of experienced middle-level lawyers doing the bulk of the work.
All of these alternative structures would substantially alter the recruit- ment and retention issues we described in Part III.

kp.k: Historical efficiency does not make current structures inevitable
kp.d: Drawing on path dependence and evolutionary theory, the authors argue that profitable institutional arrangements need not be uniquely efficient or optimal. They contrast American firms with accounting firms and European legal practices, including different employee categories, promotion systems and pricing arrangements. Competitive and technological disruption may permit reform, but outcomes are uncertain: new management structures or educational reforms could instead reproduce racial hierarchy.
qs: the original path continues to shape the debate over the future of elite firms.
The combination of these forces creates the potential for new "efficient" firm structures.
Firms that adopt more rationalized manage- ment structures may simply ghettoize black lawyers in relatively low status positions.
